(CNN) -- A Saudi Arabian blogger detained in December, ostensibly because he supported reform advocates accused by the Saudi government of backing terrorism, has been released, a fellow blogger posted Saturday. Web sites like this one pushed for Fouad al-Farhan's release. Ahmed al-Omran said on his blog, saudijeans.org, and later told CNN that he was awakened by a text message from the wife of Fouad al-Farhan, saying he had been released and was at home with his family. "That's great news, and this is just how I wanted to start my morning," al-Omran wrote. He said he later spoke with al-Farhan for several minutes on the telephone. "He sounded fine; he seems to be in good spirits," al-Omran said. "He said he would have more to talk about later but not at this point. He said now he'd like to take some time to spend with his family, with his children that he hasn't seen for so long."  Watch al-Omran describe his conversation with al-Farhan » . A Web site set up to call for al-Farhan's release said, "Fouad is free. He is back home in Jeddah after 137 days in custody." The Saudi Interior Ministry said it had no immediate comment on the reports. In January, a ministry spokesman said al-Farhan was arrested December 10 "because he violated the regulations of the kingdom." But in an e-mail posted on al-Farhan's Web site after his arrest, he told friends that he faced arrest for supporting 10 reform advocates the Saudi government accused of backing terrorism. In the e-mail, al-Farhan said a senior Interior Ministry official promised that he would remain in custody for three days at most if he agreed to sign a letter of apology. "I'm not sure if I'm ready to do that," he wrote. "An apology for what? Apologizing because I said the government is [a] liar when they accused those guys of supporting terrorism?" Al-Farhan, who blogs at alfarhan.org, is one of the few Saudi Web commentators to use his own name, according to the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists. In January, the Bush administration expressed its concerns to the Saudi government regarding al-Farhan's detention at "a relatively senior level," U.S. State Department spokesman Sean McCormack said. "The U.S. stands for freedom of expression," McCormack said at the time. "Wherever people are seeking to express themselves, via the Internet or via other areas, whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere in the world, we stand with that freedom of expression, and that was our message to the Saudi government." The American Islamic Congress, a U.S.-based nonprofit organization, launched an online letter-writing campaign aimed at freeing al-Farhan, whom it called "the godfather of Saudi blogging." "All he did was express his opinions in a very obvious way, and he didn't threaten anyone," al-Omran said. "He was advocating against violence and terrorism." Al-Omran said al-Farhan had stopped blogging for a few months in late 2006, after the Interior Ministry ordered him to take down a blog he was operating, but he began again at a new site. He said al-Farhan told him he was treated well in jail. He also called al-Farhan's release a turning point for the blogging community in Saudi Arabia. "It showed the community of bloggers in Saudi Arabia can come together and support this cause -- support his freedom of speech -- even those who didn't agree with some of the things he wrote," he said. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Mohammed Jamjoom contributed to this report.

**Headline: Voices Unsilenced: How an Online Movement Freed Saudi Arabia’s Pioneering Blogger**

In December 2007, the Saudi Arabian blogosphere experienced a seismic shock. Fouad al-Farhan, widely regarded as the "godfather" of Saudi blogging, was abruptly arrested by security forces at his office in Jeddah. Held in solitary confinement without formal charges, his crime was not a violent act, but a series of courageous posts advocating for political reform and civil liberties in a kingdom notorious for its strict control over public discourse.

Al-Farhan occupied a unique and vulnerable position in Saudi Arabia’s digital landscape. At a time when virtually all online dissidents hid behind pseudonyms to evade state surveillance, al-Farhan took the bold step of blogging under his real name. He believed that transparency was essential for genuine democratic dialogue. 

The immediate catalyst for his detention was his outspoken defense of a group of prominent academics, lawyers, and reform advocates who had been arrested in Jeddah earlier that year. The Saudi Ministry of Interior claimed the reformists were involved in funding terrorism. Al-Farhan, however, publicly challenged this narrative, arguing that the men were peaceful patriots being persecuted simply for demanding a constitutional monarchy, judicial independence, and an end to corruption. Shortly before his arrest, al-Farhan privately warned friends that officials had pressured him to apologize for his writings—a demand he steadfastly refused.

When news of his disappearance broke, it sparked an unprecedented wave of digital activism across the Middle East and the globe. Refusing to be intimidated, fellow Saudi commentators, regional bloggers, and international human rights organizations launched a coordinated public campaign titled "Free Fouad." 

Supporters created dedicated websites, flooded social media platforms with solidarity banners, and continuously tracked his case. International watchdogs, including Amnesty International, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), and Reporters Without Borders, picked up the mantle, issuing press releases and pressuring foreign governments to intervene. The movement turned al-Farhan’s case into a global symbol of the struggle for free expression in the Gulf region, making it impossible for Saudi authorities to quietly resolve the matter behind closed doors.

For four agonizing months, al-Farhan remained in custody. He was denied access to legal representation, leaving his family and supporters in constant anxiety over his health and well-being. Yet, as the international outcry grew louder, holding him became an increasingly costly public relations burden for the Saudi regime.

Finally, after 137 days of arbitrary detention, the pressure yielded results. On April 26, 2008, al-Farhan was released without charge and allowed to return home to his wife and children. 

His release was celebrated as a landmark victory for digital activism in the Arab world. It demonstrated for the first time that a decentralized, grass-roots online campaign could successfully challenge state authority in Saudi Arabia and compel the release of a high-profile political prisoner. By standing by his real name and his convictions, Fouad al-Farhan not only reunited with his family but also paved the way for a new generation of commentators seeking to broaden the boundaries of free speech in the region.

**Prominent Saudi blogger freed after years in detention, family and activists say**

By **Tamara Qiblawi** and **Kylie Atwood**, CNN  
Updated 4:12 PM EDT, Thu October 24, 2024

**(CNN) —** Youssef Al-Harthi, a prominent Saudi Arabian blogger and digital rights advocate who was imprisoned in 2018 after publicly defending detained reformists, has been released from prison, his family and human rights organizations confirmed Thursday.

Al-Harthi, 38, was served a seven-year sentence by a specialized anti-terrorism court in Riyadh on charges that included "disrupting public order," "inciting public opinion," and violating the kingdom's strict cybercrime laws. His arrest came during a sweeping crackdown on intellectuals, journalists, and civil society advocates under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

His sister, Amani Al-Harthi, posted a photo on X (formerly Twitter) on Thursday showing the blogger embracing his young son at their family home in Jeddah, captioned simply: "He is home."

Rights groups note that while Al-Harthi is no longer behind bars, he remains subject to a strict 10-year travel ban and a prohibition on publishing content online or speaking to international media.

**[RELATED VIDEO: How Saudi Arabia’s crackdown on dissent collides with its modernization drive]**

### A voice for the silenced

Al-Harthi gained international prominence in the mid-2010s through his blog, *The Reformer’s Lens*, where he documented the trials of peaceful activists, including members of the banned Saudi Civil and Political Rights Association (ACPRA). When many of his peers were detained, Al-Harthi used his platform to advocate for their legal rights and demand judicial transparency.

His release comes after years of sustained advocacy from international rights monitors and behind-the-scenes diplomatic pressure from Washington.

"Seeing Youssef back with his family brings an overwhelming sense of relief, but we must be clear-eyed about what this release actually means," said Lina Al-Hathloul, a fellow Saudi activist and head of monitoring at the UK-based human rights group ALQST. 

"Youssef was stripped of years of his life simply for writing words in defense of his countrymen," Al-Hathloul told CNN. "He is moving from a small prison to a larger one. Until his travel ban is lifted and he can speak without fear of rearrest, he is not truly free."

### Washington welcomes the move

The U.S. State Department welcomed news of Al-Harthi’s release on Thursday, describing it as a positive step while reiterating calls for Saudi Arabia to address broader human rights concerns.

"The United States welcomes the release of Youssef Al-Harthi from prison," a senior State Department official said in a statement to CNN. "We have consistently raised Mr. Al-Harthi’s case at the highest levels of the Saudi government. While this is a welcome development, we continue to urge the Saudi leadership to lift restrictions on freedom of expression and remove travel bans imposed on individuals who have served their sentences."

The Biden administration has faced ongoing scrutiny over its balancing act between strategic security and energy cooperation with Riyadh and its stated commitment to holding the kingdom accountable for human rights abuses following the 2018 murder of *Washington Post* columnist Jamal Khashoggi.

**[RELATED VIDEO: Biden's evolving relationship with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman]**

### A climate of calculated tolerance

Saudi Arabia has spent recent years attempting to reshape its global image through grand economic initiatives, mega-projects like NEOM, and massive investments in global sports. However, rights organizations contend that the kingdom’s social reforms have been accompanied by an unprecedented tightening of political control.

Activists note that releases of high-profile political prisoners in Saudi Arabia are often timed around major diplomatic summits or strategic negotiations. 

"Saudi authorities frequently use these conditional releases to alleviate international diplomatic pressure," said Sarah Leah Whitson, executive director of Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN). "Yet, the machinery of repression remains completely intact."

The Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Saudi Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment regarding the terms of Al-Harthi’s release.

According to ALQST, dozens of Saudi bloggers, journalists, and peaceful commentators remain imprisoned or subject to severe sentence extensions for social media posts deemed critical of the government.

***

*CNN’s Sarah El Sirgany contributed to this report from Cairo, and Jennifer Hansler contributed from Washington.*

After 137 days of detainment without formal charges, prominent Saudi blogger Fouad al-Farhan has been released from custody by Saudi authorities. Al-Farhan, widely considered the father of the Saudi blogosphere, was released in Jeddah, bringing an end to a high-profile detention that sparked unprecedented online activism and drawn international diplomatic scrutiny.

Al-Farhan was arrested on December 10, 2007, at his office in Jeddah by Saudi security officials. Prior to his arrest, al-Farhan had prepared an email to be sent to friends if he was detained, explaining that authorities had targeted him for advocating on behalf of political prisoners—specifically ten reformists arrested earlier that year—and for pushing the boundaries of free speech in the Kingdom through his personal blog.

### A Landmark Digital Campaign: #FreeFouad

Al-Farhan’s arrest sent shockwaves through the Middle East’s burgeoning digital landscape. Almost immediately, fellow writers and digital activists launched the "Free Fouad" campaign. 

Website owners across the Arab world and beyond displayed "Free Fouad" banners, blacked out their avatars, and utilized social media platforms and RSS feeds to keep his case in the global spotlight. The campaign marked a turning point for digital rights in the region, demonstrating the ability of online networks to mobilize around human rights issues despite state censorship.

Ahmed al-Omran, a leading Saudi blogger who tracked the case extensively on his influential blog *saudijeans.org*, expressed immense relief and joy upon news of the release.

"This is a great day for the Saudi blogosphere," al-Omran wrote on *saudijeans.org*, reflecting the collective mood of the online community. "Fouad's release proves that our voices matter and that standing up for one another is not in vain. He became a symbol of our struggle for free expression, and having him back with his family is a victory for all of us."

Al-Omran emphasized that while al-Farhan’s release was a cause for celebration, the campaign highlighted the ongoing vulnerabilities faced by digital writers in the country.

### International Scrutiny and U.S. Reaction

The detention of al-Farhan attracted significant international media coverage and placed pressure on foreign governments allied with Riyadh, particularly the United States. Under the Bush administration, the U.S. State Department repeatedly raised concerns regarding al-Farhan’s status, framing his detention as a setback for political and civil reform in the Middle East.

Following the announcement of his release, the State Department issued an official response welcoming the news. 

"We are pleased to hear that Fouad al-Farhan has been released," stated State Department spokesman Sean McCormack. The Bush administration had previously noted that the arrest of peaceful bloggers ran counter to the broader goals of openness and reform that Washington had urged regional partners to adopt.

### A Legacy for Arab Cyber-Activism

Al-Farhan’s release without charges is seen by observers as a rare concession by Saudi security authorities in response to public and international pressure. Upon returning home, al-Farhan expressed gratitude to the global community of bloggers and supporters who kept his name alive throughout his nearly four and a half months in solitary confinement and interrogation.

While al-Farhan's detainment underscored the risks faced by dissidents in the region, his 137-day ordeal ultimately solidified the role of the internet as a powerful platform for accountability, forever altering the landscape of Saudi civic engagement.

**CNN.com** — *INTERNATIONAL*

**DATELINE: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (April 26, 2008)** 

In a landmark development for human rights and digital activism in the Middle East, Fouad al-Farhan—widely regarded as the "godfather of Saudi blogging"—has been released from prison after nearly five months of detention without charge. 

Al-Farhan, 33, was released late Saturday night from the Maximum Security Dhahban Prison near Jeddah, according to family members and human rights advocates in Riyadh. His freedom marks the end of a high-profile standoff between a new generation of tech-savvy reformists and Saudi Arabia’s powerful security apparatus.

For four and a half months, al-Farhan’s empty blog site, *Al-Farhan.org*, stood as a silent testament to the fraught boundaries of speech in the ultra-conservative kingdom. Today, his release is being hailed by free-speech advocates as a watershed moment for the Arab digital sphere.

### The Arrest: Pushing the Boundaries of Digital Speech

Al-Farhan was taken into custody on December 10, 2007, by officials from the Saudi Interior Ministry. Before his arrest, al-Farhan realized he was being targeted and posted a final, prophetic message to his colleagues, instructing them to publish a pre-written statement if he disappeared. 

In that statement, al-Farhan revealed that Saudi security officials had warned him to stop advocating for a group of political dissidents known as the "Jeddah Reformists"—a group of academics and lawyers arrested in early 2007 for calling for a constitutional monarchy. 

While the Saudi Interior Ministry officially stated al-Farhan was held for "interrogation regarding non-written violations of non-penal regulations"—a vague administrative terminology often used for security detentions—analysts say his true "crime" was breaking the unwritten rules of Saudi media. 

Unlike traditional journalists who operate under strict state censorship, al-Farhan used his blog, written in accessible Arabic, to openly discuss political reform, government corruption, and the plight of political detainees. He argued that loyalty to the kingdom did not require absolute silence regarding its faults. 

### The Refusal to Apologize: A Test of Principles

Crucial to al-Farhan’s ordeal—and his ultimate rise as an icon of resistance—was his refusal to sign a formal letter of apology and an undertaking (*istichdad*) promising to permanently cease his online commentary. 

Sources close to the family tell CNN that during the early weeks of his detention, security officials offered al-Farhan a swift release in exchange for a public recantation of his views and a pledge never to blog again. Al-Farhan steadfastly refused, insisting he had violated no written laws and refusing to trade his political principles for his freedom.

His defiance prolonged his imprisonment, but it elevated his case from a local police matter to an international cause célèbre. 

Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and the U.S. State Department repeatedly raised his case with Saudi authorities. Online, a global grass-roots campaign under the banner "#FreeFouad" spread across the nascent blogosphere and social networks, turning al-Farhan into a symbol of a movement that the Saudi government could neither censor nor easily control.

### A Major Turning Point for Free Expression

Media analysts and Saudi observers say al-Farhan’s release without a trial or formal conviction marks a crucial turning point for the kingdom's digital landscape for several reasons:

**1. The Failure of Traditional Censorship:** 
Historically, the Saudi Ministry of Information controlled the flow of news by shutting down newspapers or banning journalists. Al-Farhan’s case demonstrated the limits of state control in the internet age. By arresting him, the authorities inadvertently amplified his voice globally, creating a phenomena known as the "backfire effect."

**2. A Precedent for Digital Citizens:** 
Had al-Farhan been quietly broken and forced into silence, it would have sent a chilling message to the thousands of young Saudis taking to the web to express themselves. His unconditional release—and his refusal to back down—signals that the government cannot easily silence digital citizens through prolonged administrative detention without incurring immense diplomatic and reputational costs.

**3. The Rising Influence of the Youth Demographic:** 
Over 60% of the Saudi population is under the age of 30. Al-Farhan represented a modern, educated, and deeply patriotic Saudi youth who want to reform the system from within, rather than overthrow it. His release suggests that elements within the Saudi leadership recognize that cracking down on moderate, modernizing voices may do more to destabilize the nation than allow for controlled digital debate.

### Moving Forward

Speaking briefly to supporters outside his home in Jeddah following his release, a fatigued but resolute al-Farhan thanked his family, his legal team, and the global network of bloggers who campaigned on his behalf. 

While it remains unclear whether al-Farhan will face ongoing travel bans or restrictions on his online activities, his return home sends a powerful signal across the Gulf. 

The battle for the Saudi public square is no longer taking place in state-approved newspapers or behind closed palace doors. It is happening online—and as the case of Fouad al-Farhan proves, the voices of the kingdom's digital generation are becoming increasingly difficult to silence.
